absent: Pids group layout and css alloc and free behaviour, parent traversal helper, charge and uncharge and cancel helpers, watermark update helper, and css resolution helpers.
Numeric value of the pids ceiling, unlimited keyword spelling details beyond its role, event enum values, error number values, and cftype flag semantics.
Cgroup core guarantees for taskset iteration, attach ordering, fork and release call order, css lifetime and pinning, and threaded mode effects.
Full rdma cgroup and device object layouts, resource type enum values and counts, css reference counting rules, and unlimited encoding rationale.
Complete rdma control file table beyond the truncated max entry, and kernfs and seq file mechanics for reads, writes and notifications.
Hierarchy root handling, unified versus legacy detection, root local events flag semantics, notification delivery guarantees, and log output destinations.
Token matching and integer parsing helper behaviour, option argument limits, allocation helpers, and list and container primitives.

findings.text: The pids controller exposes its lifecycle through a subsystem descriptor that binds allocation, fork admission and cancellation, attach admission and cancellation, and release handlers, selects distinct control file sets for legacy versus unified hierarchies, and marks itself as supporting threaded mode.

Fork admission resolves the destination pids group from the incoming css set, attempts a hierarchical charge of one entry, and on failure records a fork reject event before propagating the refusal; success leaves the charge in place for later cancellation or release.

Task migration charges the destination group and uncharges the origin group for each moved task while relying on core cgroup pinning for the origin state; the cancellation path performs the inverse transfer to restore prior accounting.

Charging walks from the target group toward the hierarchy root, atomically adding the requested count and comparing against each ancestor limit, updating a high watermark on the successful prefix, and on the first over limit ancestor unwinding all prior additions including the failing node and signalling exhaustion with EAGAIN while identifying the failing ancestor.

The maximum file accepts a short unlimited keyword meaning the largest representable pid count, otherwise a numeric string that must be non negative and below that ceiling; updates store atomically without serialising against concurrent forks, and display shows the keyword when at ceiling else the decimal value.

Current reflects the live atomic count, peak reflects a separately maintained watermark observed through a single load, and the event view reports either a local fork failure tally or hierarchical maximum tallies depending on hierarchy flavour and a root flag selecting local event mode.

A task count moves from uncharged to charged at fork admission, then either back to uncharged on fork cancellation or attach rollback, forward to a new group on successful migration, or back to uncharged at release; failed charges never leave partial hierarchy state.
A per resource record carries three signed integers representing the configured ceiling, the current in use count, and the historical peak count.

A device pool associates one device pointer with a fixed array of per resource records, membership in both a per cgroup list and a per device list, an aggregate active use total, a count of resources currently set to unlimited, and four per resource event tallies distinguishing hierarchical versus local and limit hit versus allocation failure.

Pools are looked up by device within a cgroup and allocated on demand with all ceilings unlimited and fresh list membership; they persist while aggregate use is non zero, while any ceiling is bounded, or while any peak or event tally remains non zero, otherwise they are unlinked from both lists and freed.
Updating a single ceiling maintains a count of unlimited entries by incrementing when entering unlimited from bounded and decrementing when leaving unlimited, then storing the new ceiling.

A single global mutex guards the device list and every pool lookup, creation, destruction, charge, uncharge, limit update and readout; lookup and mutation helpers assert the mutex is held, while public charge, uncharge, register, unregister and file operations acquire it around the critical section.

Pids accounting uses per group atomic 64 bit counters and limits with atomic add and test for admission and atomic stores for limit changes, plus a single load read for the watermark, with no mutex shown in these fragments for charge, display or migration paths.

Charge pins the current cgroup, validates the resource index, then charges one unit along the ancestor chain creating pools as needed and refusing with resource exhaustion if any ceiling would be exceeded; peaks advance only after the whole chain succeeds, failure emits hierarchical and local events and unwinds the partial prefix before dropping the pin.

Uncharge ignores out of range resource selectors, otherwise walks from the charged group up to but excluding a stop point decrementing use and aggregate totals, freeing idle unlimited history free pools, and finally releases one css reference.

Limit writes strip surrounding whitespace, take a leading device name, then accept an optional numeric device index plus per resource numeric or unlimited assignments, rejecting repeated indexes, negative numbers, unknown tokens, unknown devices and ambiguous names without index; successful updates adjust per resource ceilings and unlimited counts and may garbage collect a newly idle unlimited history free pool.

Status, peak and event reads hold the global mutex, iterate all registered devices, print each device key with a numeric disambiguator only when the name collides, then emit per resource values or event tallies with unlimited shown as a keyword and missing pools shown as unlimited ceilings and zero use, peak and events.

Breach accounting increments local failure in the requester and local maximum in the over limit group when pools exist, then walks each ancestor chain creating pools as needed and skipping increments only when creation fails, notifying the corresponding event files for every successful update.

Devices start with fresh empty pool and global list nodes, become visible only after insertion under lock, and on removal are first unlinked under lock so no new pools can attach before all existing pools for that device are destroyed while still holding the lock.

Decrementing a resource with no pool for the device warns about the invalid combination and returns without altering state, and a decrement that would make a use count negative triggers a one time warning while still applying the decrement, signalling a caller accounting bug.

On limit breach the forking group increments a local fork failure tally and logs once, then either notifies local files in legacy or local event mode or records a local maximum in the over limit group and propagates hierarchical maximum counts upward with per group notifications.
The rdma controller publishes operations to attempt hierarchical charge returning the pinned group, to release a hierarchical charge, and to publish or withdraw a device from global accounting.

Helper conversions derive a rdma cgroup from a subsystem state via container linkage, fetch a parent cgroup through the subsystem parent pointer, and pin the current task group through the task css accessor.

Device resolution scans the global list for name matches, returns immediately on name plus index match, reports ambiguity when a bare name matches more than one entry, and reports absence when nothing matches; name uniqueness is determined by scanning for a distinct entry with the same name.

Pids exposes control entries named max, current, peak and events on both flavours plus events dot local on unified only, with max writable and the others read only, events entries bound to per group notification slots, and all entries hidden from the hierarchy root.

Rdma resource vocabulary uses two names for handle and object resources, an unlimited keyword spelled max, limit tokens for optional numeric index and per resource numeric or unlimited values, and three read selectors distinguishing ceiling, current and peak views; numeric ceilings use 32 bit signed maxima for unlimited and the max file is writable, readable as ceiling view, and hidden from root.
